sections.section: Structural and Kinematic Evolution at Cosmic Noon

claims.text: A large fraction of resolved, massive star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (z~1-3) are rotation-dominated but dynamically hot, turbulent disks in emission-line integral-field data.
Intrinsic ionized-gas velocity dispersions are elevated at high redshift and decline toward lower redshift, with sigma_0 ~ 50 km/s at z~2.3 falling to ~25 km/s at z~0.9 in mass-selected disk samples.

At fixed stellar mass, star-forming galaxies are smaller at higher redshift, with rest-optical effective radius scaling roughly as (1+z)^-0.75 for late types and more steeply (~(1+z)^-1.48) for quiescent galaxies over 0 < z < 3.

Kiloparsec-scale star-forming clumps with inferred masses of order 10^7-10^9 solar masses are common in resolved images and line maps of gas-rich high-redshift disks, though PSF blending and SED assumptions can strongly inflate the masses.

In dynamical models, the inner regions (within roughly one effective radius) of many massive cosmic-noon disks are baryon dominated, with low inferred central dark-matter fractions (median f_DM ~ 8% for a Chabrier IMF in some samples).
Broad ionized-gas emission components reveal galaxy-scale outflows in normal (non-AGN-selected) star-forming samples at cosmic noon, common in incidence even where the mass flux remains uncertain.

Bulge growth, dense central cores, and compact star-forming systems are observationally linked to structural pathways toward quiescence, though progenitor matching is statistical rather than object-by-object proof.

Whether most massive main-sequence star-forming galaxies are ordered rotating disks or whether disturbed systems and mergers make up a comparably important fraction is unresolved, because resolution, depth, kinematic classification, and pair timescales prevent a universal fraction.
claims.debate_topic: Disks versus mergers among massive cosmic-noon star-forming galaxies

claims.text: The physical driver of elevated high-redshift disk turbulence is contested between gravitational instability and accretion versus stellar-feedback energy and momentum injection.

Whether giant star-forming clumps are long-lived bound structures that migrate inward to build bulges or short-lived features disrupted by feedback is unresolved, as inferred ages and masses are resolution- and model-dependent.

Whether low inferred inner dark-matter fractions reflect genuine baryon dominance or are artifacts of pressure support, IMF and gas-mass assumptions, halo contraction or cores, and sample selection is unresolved, since rotation curves rarely extend far beyond the luminous disk and mass components are degenerate.
claims.debate_topic: Reality of low inner dark-matter fractions at cosmic noon

claims.text: Whether galaxies reach quiescence through central compaction before quenching or through gradual inside-out disk growth with bulge buildup is debated, because cross-sectional populations do not uniquely reconstruct evolutionary tracks.
claims.debate_topic: Compaction versus inside-out growth toward quenching

sections.section: The Star-Forming Main Sequence and Quenching

claims.text: Main-sequence star formation dominates the cosmic-noon star-formation-rate budget, with strong starburst outliers contributing only a minority of the total.

Whether the star-forming main sequence is near-linear or bent with a high-mass flattening, and how its slope and normalization evolve with redshift, is unresolved because SFR indicators, dust corrections, IMF, selection, stacking, and bulge contamination shift the fits.

Massive main-sequence galaxies at z~1-3 contain large molecular-gas reservoirs with shorter depletion times than local disks, of order 0.7-1.0 Gyr, subject to CO excitation and alpha_CO or dust-to-gas calibration systematics.

sections.section: Stellar Population Synthesis and Stellar-Mass Systematics

claims.text: A stellar-population-synthesis prediction combines an initial mass function, stellar-evolution isochrones, and stellar spectra to form simple stellar populations, then convolves them with a star-formation history, enrichment, and dust for composite populations, so every inferred quantity inherits the adopted ingredients and priors.
Stellar mass is among the more robust SED-derived galaxy properties, but it remains a model-dependent mass-to-light scaling set by the adopted SPS ingredients rather than a direct observation.

The low-mass normalization of the IMF strongly controls stellar mass-to-light ratios while contributing little integrated light, so that a large fraction (roughly 60-80%) of stellar mass can reside in low-mass stars that are nearly invisible in the SED.

Old-population optical colors and many absorption indices suffer a strong age-metallicity degeneracy, in which an age change of roughly a factor of three mimics a metallicity change of a factor of two, requiring high signal-to-noise full spectra to partially break it.

The treatment of the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant-branch phase drives large near-infrared SPS differences for intermediate-age (~0.1-2 Gyr) populations, whereas optical color-based mass-to-light estimates are generally less sensitive to the TP-AGB prescription.

Extinction and attenuation laws are neither interchangeable nor universal, because dust geometry and stellar age alter the effective attenuation across Milky-Way sightlines, starbursts, and normal galaxies.

Ultraviolet-continuum, recombination-line, and infrared star-formation-rate indicators average star formation over different timescales and dust sensitivities, with UV continuum tracing roughly the last ~100 Myr and Halpha the last <~10 Myr under a steady-state IMF assumption.

Whether the intermediate-age near-infrared contribution of TP-AGB stars is heavy or comparatively light is unresolved, because cluster calibrators, stochasticity, metallicity, star-formation history, and circumstellar dust permit competing fits.
claims.debate_topic: Strength of the TP-AGB contribution in SPS models

claims.text: Whether the stellar IMF is effectively universal and Milky-Way-like or varies systematically with galaxy velocity dispersion or abundance is debated, with gravity-sensitive spectra, dynamics, and lensing of massive early-type galaxies suggesting heavier normalizations but remaining degenerate with abundance responses and dark matter.
claims.debate_topic: IMF universality versus systematic variation across galaxies

claims.text: Whether simple exponential or rising parametric star-formation histories or nonparametric burst-capable reconstructions better recover galaxy properties is unresolved, since flexible models reduce bias but increase prior dependence and time-bin covariance.

Whether absolute stellar masses are accurate at roughly the factor-of-two level or are limited by larger SPS, IMF, and SFH systematics is debated, because formal fit errors omit model mismatch and unseen old or low-mass populations, and extreme SFH choices can shift recovered mass by up to ~0.6 dex.
The central-galaxy stellar-to-halo mass relation is strongly non-linear, with the maximum integrated galaxy-formation efficiency near a Milky-Way-scale halo of about 10^12 solar masses.
At z~0 the peak integrated stellar-mass efficiency, defined as central stellar mass divided by the cosmic baryon allotment of the halo, remains below about 20% (roughly 0.15-0.20 near the pivot).
The intrinsic scatter in central stellar mass at fixed halo mass above the pivot is small, generally below about 0.2 dex, and usually modeled as lognormal after removing measurement errors.
Below the pivot halo mass, central stellar mass falls steeply with decreasing halo mass, and the slope and scatter of the relation become increasingly uncertain toward the dwarf regime.
At group and cluster halo masses, central stellar mass grows much more slowly than halo mass, roughly as M_h^(1/3), once BCG photometry and intracluster light are accounted for.

Halo occupation distribution and conditional luminosity function models require separate central and satellite occupation distributions to reproduce galaxy abundance and scale-dependent clustering, with the one-halo/two-halo transition producing measurable departures from a single clustering power law.

Abundance matching can reproduce galaxy abundance and clustering by rank-ordering galaxies against halos and subhalos using a chosen proxy with scatter, subject to assumptions about monotonicity, proxy choice, orphans, disruption, and stellar-mass systematics.
In collisionless simulations, dark-matter halo clustering depends on formation history and concentration at fixed halo mass, a phenomenon termed halo assembly bias.

Satellite-galaxy star formation and color differ from those of comparable central galaxies, and reconstructed infall histories imply a delayed then relatively rapid quenching (delay of order 2-4 Gyr followed by an e-folding time <~0.8 Gyr) for local massive satellites.

Whether the galaxy-halo connection is adequately described by mass-only halo occupation or requires explicit coupling of galaxy properties to halo formation history or concentration (galaxy assembly bias) is unresolved, because halo masses and secondary properties are noisy and correlated and environment can mimic the signal.

The dominant origin of scatter in the stellar-to-halo mass relation, among merger and accretion history, concentration, spin, baryonic stochasticity, and measurement error, is debated, because inferred intrinsic scatter depends on deconvolution and cross-correlated galaxy observables.

The optimal halo proxy for abundance matching, whether present Vmax or mass, peak velocity or mass, infall values, or compound concentration-sensitive proxies, is unresolved, since satellite stripping, disruption, resolution, and orphan galaxies change small-scale clustering.

The physical mechanism of satellite quenching, among starvation or strangulation, ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, and preprocessing with different timing, is unresolved, because demographics constrain delay and fade times better than a unique physical mechanism.
